They had a party for the benefit of underprivileged Jewish children, I think, or something like that. And I was engaged to play on the president for that occasion. And I played on the boat a couple times with Paul Barberin, but I never did make those excursions that you were fine to. I never did make those. I mean, just never get around to it.
Did you ever work with Paul Barberin when he had a small New Orleans-style jazz band?
Mm-hmm.
Except lately, of course. I mean, the last couple years ago you were with him.

Yeah, I worked with him a couple years ago on Clevester. Oh, he worked at Dream Room over at the Pier 600. He worked at Mardi Gras with him. And I worked at Paddock with him on the regular band off night. I don't think Paul ever worked at the Paddock regular. Who would be in the band? Oh, in Paul's band? Mm-hmm. He had Picky on trumpet. John Brunus, we call him Picky. And Trombone. The same trombone he's got now. Turbillon. Clemens Turbillon. And Willie Humphrey on clarinet. The same setup he's got now.
Just a different bass.
Yeah. Santiago. That's right. The San... Barnell on the... I mean, not Barnell. Black.
Yeah.
Leicester. That's his right there. Leicester, Santiago.
Did you ever work with Barnell?
Oh, Lil' Barham jobs. I mean...
Barnell. Could he play?

Could he play? His bass is alive. He's a boogie-woogie. Yeah, he played a lot of piano. I mean, he was... I'd say just naturally gifted because he couldn't read. But he could... He could improvise so well. And then... Then Barnell had such a keen ear. He could work in anybody's band. And I don't care what kind of modulation you make, he'll change key along with you. Just the same as if he was reading. As a matter of fact, I recall one time, I think it was on the Pelican, when the Pelican was open, that Earl Hines came down and he and Boynell got titled down a piano contest and he gave him a drill. He really was great.
Would you call him Barrel House, Tonk style, or would you say that he played like anybody in particular, or what?

Well, he had... He was another individualist. He had a style of his own. He was more or less on a boogie-woogie style. But he also played some nice blues. And occasionally, he played a pretty nice ballad. But he was really a boogie-woogie piano player. I'd call him that. He was a boogie-woogie man.
Had a good lead hand.
Yeah. He had a good two-hand.
I never got to hear it. When did you first lead your own band?
Oh, that wasn't too long ago. It must have been around... 54, 55 I had a Dixon Lane outfit.
Who'd you have with it?
Clemens Tervalon, Wallace Davenport, Saeed. What's Saeed right now? Frazier. Frazier on drums. Oh, a couple of times I had Emma Barry on piano with me.
Clarin' that old girl.
Oh, Clarin' that was hard to keep up with. I mean, having a regular band. I had one time, this fellow that died after a kid, Ernest.
Mm-hmm. Ernest Moya.
Ernest Moya, yeah. He worked with me. Wow. Howard Dejan work with me several times.
On what instrument was he on?
Saxophone. And Mr. Fatty, Louie Contrell, he played a couple times with me. That's our president, local president. You know.
Ever used Kit Howard or Paul Barnes?
Yeah, the kid played a couple times with me too. He played a couple of jobs I had, Jackson Barracks and a couple other spots I, you know, booked them on.
What about Noon?
Well, Noon and Sam and I, we, we clowned around for quite a while in between band working. I mean, Noon and Sam and I played a trio worked out at the Lafitte Hotel for quite a while.
Told you you had some propit down there. You had some propit down there.
Well, no, we worked, just the three of us. we had to play and sing like that with Sam on the guitar and Noon with the bazooka and me with the bass ball.
Ever have Kid Clayton and Sam Lee outside?

Well, yeah, Clayton's worked with me too but not, not together with Noon and Sam. I mean, as a matter of fact, Clayton will be working with me Mardi Gras there. I have my own job Mardi Gras there right here on Royal Street at the American League in Coni and Ro. And I got Kid Clayton with me on that job. Kid Clayton, Harold De Jong, Sae, Eddie Summers on trombone, Smitty on piano.
Smitty.
Yeah.
Sounds familiar. I can't place it.
You know, Smitty, Smitty works, most of the time he works, he works with, with Harold De Jong.
You say Harold De Jong is now with Lawrence Marrero's band?

Well, no, he's, he's working Saturday on this job because Paul is out of town. but he's not an official member as yet. I expect Paul back soon. Well, Paul's supposed to be back for Christmas. I'm positive he'll be back for Carnival because he's, he's only, he's only, he's only supposed to be on a, on a business trip more or less.
Which band have you enjoyed working with, more than I'm trying to put you on the spot but do you like big bands or little bands? Which have been your most enjoyable jobs? Well, I don't know. I mean,

I really like big band work but, the financial difference you get in big bands make you change your mind so, minds change for the sake of the greenbacks. I mean, so, I, I like little band work. As a matter of fact, I, I, I like something I have never done before. I'd like to get with a string ensemble if I can but I, I haven't as yet taken the time to try to find the, the proper musicians to, to make up a string ensemble. But, I like Dixieland.
What do you mean string ensemble? Guitar and bass? Guitar, bass, violin,
and piano, well, naturally. But, no, no blowing instruments at all. Yeah. It's a string ensemble.
Maybe we can do

something about that. But, the only thing, I mean, in New Orleans, it's so hard to keep a band unless you can find work. And right now, I don't know what, what avenue to start looking for work for a string ensemble. I mean, nobody's particular about it. I mean, right now, the rock and roll got things sold up so badly until, it's kind of hard. that's one kind of music. That's one kind of music.

I mean I'll play it because it paid me but I prefer Dixon Land for actual personal enjoyment you might say. Well I mean I like ballads thrown along in there but I mean actually for what you call stomped down jumping, a good Dixon Land band you just can't get around because you always have that absolute beat and that's very essential with that type of music.

In regard to your bass, do you notice that the New Orleans players on bass play different than other styles of music? Is there any certain style that you'd say makes the Dixieland rather than ordinary big band bass? I'd say that Ellington, of course your cousin played in Ellington too, but I mean ordinarily is there any difference?

Well I mean the average Dixieland bass player as I notice as I gather, he's always playing the root of the chord, I mean it's just, you have to, to make it fit in right. Now if you take a big band, after a band gets to be around 12 pieces or more, well whoever's arranging can take the bass off the basic note of the chord and place it somewhere else according to how he's voicing, how he's voicing his instrumentation. And sometimes you hear a bass playing completely almost off the chord if you, unless you just actually know the arrangement and know how it's built. But Dixieland, the bass, we always call it, I mean I do call it the bottom, he always stays in the cellar, he's always bringing the basic note of the particular chord that's supposed to be played.

When you think of your job in a band, in a small Dixieland band, do you think of it more like that? To keep the beat going or is it to fill in the harmony of the chords or what do you think of yourself?

Well I mean I like to keep the beat going but I like to keep the right chords going too because I mean it's very effective. I mean a lot of people don't realize it, probably I mean people unless they're musicians wouldn't know the difference. But I mean it's a big difference if you're playing just as simple, I would say something in C. And you got a bass man up there that probably is not paying attention to what he's doing or maybe they'll know what he's doing, I'll put it that way too. And you playing something in C, he's reaching down there and playing a D flat, a big D flat against a C major chord, well I mean that don't work out at all, no kind of way. And it's very important for the bass to, especially in Dixieland, to keep the basic note of the chord going at all times regardless. Because if the public could know what the musician he's playing was he'll let them know maybe after they get through the number they'll let them know in not such a sweet tongue.

Now when you play, well say all New Orleans bass players, take them for example, you know that they tend to play in first position, second position along and there or do they play it down below the seventh position or whatever it is on the bass?

Oh well that all depends on the bass player itself. I mean the majority of New Orleans bass players, I mean they tend to play in first to third position most of the time. But sometimes the number gets loose and you feel like showing off or you run around there because I mean I do it a lot of times myself. Well just like this Dixieland is supposed to be, you play it according to how you feel. If you feel like running down in case of them high notes, well I mean it's effective, it's very nice too.
What about solos on the bass? In the old days did they ever take many bass solos? They do occasionally now. Do you think it's a good idea?

Well, I couldn't boast it as a good idea. Then probably is a good idea because I like bass solos myself at times but I'm not a bass soloist. I mean I'm very clumsy when it comes to playing a bass solo because if they give me a solo, the only thing I will do with it is to keep up the beat and maintain the chord progression for the particular number that's being played. But as far as picking a melody or something through the number, I mean I've never, probably it's just my lack of practice of doing it that way but I never did, I never could make it fit in. And so for that reason I never did promote myself as a bass solos, I never was.
Well who was the star during that when you were a kid?

What bass soloist? Well this fellow I told you about before, he got killed at sea. Cleo? Cleo had a wonderful slap. Well at that time it was a novelty to play slap bass. Very much novelty because he used to play it with a triplet effect. I've seen you do that. Yeah I couldn't do it but I mean I've gotten out of practice because slap bass is just about out of style. Now you better tell them here anybody playing slap bass. Not even when you're picking. If your bass is strong so that the string is going to slap back on you. Some fellows got such a heavy pull, they have to raise their strings higher than others. That's to avoid the slap back that the string will give. But the back you don't ever hear any bass player playing slap bass anymore.
In the slap bass do you actually take your hand and hit the string against the fingerboard or even it snaps back?

You do it both ways. You slap your hand on the bass bass and you pull the string out very hard and let it slap back and then you come right back with a slap that makes the three licks and it'll be done real fair. And give you a triplet effect. And Cleo was exceptionally great on that. It was nice doing that time because it was just something new. People liked it just like the same as any other novelty. It comes out and it's good when it first started. And after a while it dies out just like anything else.
What did he take? Two bars? Or 12 bars? Or 16 bars?

Or 32? Or what? Cleo. Oh, he'd take the whole course. He'd play all night long if they'd just let him. His band just had to come on in and take him out because he gets good to him and he just works with it.
By what year was that? How old was that?

Cleo was popular from I'd say as far as I can remember from around 29 or 30 up until the war started. He got killed on a merchant ship because he went to the merchant marine and the ship he was on was bombed somewhere out of sea. But he was very popular around New Orleans as a bass player. Very nice bass player. I used to like his playing and I used to like his solo work because I just like that slap effect he had. I mean I can slap a little but I never could perfect it as well as Cleo. He is real good. I think Chester can do a little of that kind of work too. Chester's always. Chester's good at straight picking and he's wonderful on the bull. And he's got a way of picking with the end of his bull. He turns his bull backwards and you pick with it like a stick in. A little frog down the screen. That's right.
What kind of a bow do you use, what they call the French style like a violin or the German where you put your hand in?
No, I used the French style. I did. A little while I did play.
Sort of like that.
That's right.
Not this one. Not the German. No.

I like that from this old German professor that was teaching at Grimmauld, Fink. He died. The violin player was he? Professor Fink. Yeah, he was teaching bass over there. And I took a few lessons with him to develop my boy. I liked quite a bit but I mean I never did practice it because I didn't have no use for it. I mean the kind of music I play, I mean you don't ever have no call for no boy.
Were you in the service? Did you get the Gihan Bell for doing that?
I was in the Navy for three and a half years. I was in the Sam band with Bill Humphrey and Clark Kerr, Magnus Kruster, we all was in the Sam Navy band together.
Well I was going to ask, you mentioned these red books, is that the Redback Book of Rags?
No, the military march books. Marches, I didn't know. Yeah, the school kids get them a lot of times. Now I mean I think you get hold of a red book when you get to about the second or third grade
of music.
That's what I wanted to make clear on that. That's mostly military marches.
There had been some old ragtime books that Fess and all of them talk about calling the Redback Oh no, I wasn't referring to that.
I was talking about the school book, I mean the musical school, I mean the second grade of music you run into red books.

You also mentioned running at tuba, did you ever play tuba much? Oh yeah, I mean that was my first session. I played a lot of orchestra with tuba. You were going to ask about brass bands out on the street, did you ever play any tubas?

Oh yeah, I played with old man Allen across the river before he died, Red Allen's daddy. And I played the street parade with the Joy Williams band. The tuxedos I played a couple times with them. And there was another old man Parker, I played with him a couple times, the old drummer. He's out of the music, he's out of all games now, he's just about too old to get around. The old man Parker lived down on St. Phil Street.
Willie Parker.

Willie Parker, that's his man. I think the last parade I played was Willie Parker. The last carnival parade I played for the Eleanor Club. I think the last parade they had before the war, after I came out of service, I don't think I fooled with it. Well after I came out of service in 45 I played with Mr. Allen, old man Allen across the river, a couple of fumes, a few parades. And with George Williams I played.
Did you ever make any records?
With Brass Band?
Any kind of records.
You mentioned Peace Show.
Well yeah I cut a few with the Fast Peace Show and I cut records with them.
You got any of the Paul Barberin? No I didn't cut those labels with Paul.
When Paul cut those labels in California I didn't go on that trip.
Did you ever make any records for Southland?

Those records I told you about made with Jeanette and Jim Robinson, George Lewis, Paul Barberin. But I don't think those records were ever released. I don't know what happened to them. I know we made them. We went up there one day and we cut about six sides or something. Four either six sides. Had a couple of them that Jeanette sang. But after it was released I don't know because I never did hear them anywhere. Of course I made a lot of records when I was in service but they wasn't for the general public. I don't know if it was Uncle Sam himself or if he was a private consign. But we used to cut them right here at the New Orleans Naval Air Station. Every Friday. Every Friday. We had a radio show we did out there. We had a radio show. We did out there. Bob Poole was master ceremony.
We had a radio show. Bob Poole was master ceremony.

And every Friday we had a radio show. And every Friday we did a show. And well for a while out there we had Robert Till. We had a radio show. We had a radio show. We had a radio show. We had a radio show. We had a radio show. We had a radio show. And every Friday we had a radio show. And every Friday we did a show. And well for a while out there we had Robert Till. He was a lieutenant then I think. Lieutenant J.G. And he he fit in a couple times for master ceremonies. When he was in service. We cut a lot of records for overseas. But didn't it. Like I said it wasn't for sale. It was a stick like a sound.
Remember any tunes you cut with Jeanette and them? Or Joe Morales?
Or the name of them? Oh I forgot the name of them.
I guess that's been a while back. Not too long ago.
About maybe three years. Something like that.

I was going to ask a little bit about your bass again. You used three quarter size you said. We didn't get all that on the tape I don't think. Oh yeah. You say you don't like the electric bass. No I don't like the electric bass. I mean I'll try them but.
You want to get the true tone to my ear. Out of a amplified bass.
Did you ever try a five string bass? There was a K5 string there. You used with an extra high string.

Yeah I tried that. I played on it but I mean I never used it for my personal stuff. A lot of the bells around here was taken off the E string. Because the E string is so deep. And it's not too very effective. Especially with the.

a big band, a loud dixieland band, so they eliminated the E and brought the A back and stepped and put the C where the G was. I didn't care much for that either. I don't guess too many of them doing it. Somewhere I played not too long ago felt like a bass drum like that.
Do you like a pretty big bass then? At least three-quarter size?
Oh yeah, I like a three-quarter. I mean, I like to get my hands on a full-size bass eventually.
Is it a bigger tone? Do you have to work harder? Does it mean working easier on it so you don't have to work so hard to get a big tone?
Well, I actually work hard. I just, I mean, I always did play a heavy bass. Always did. I don't say I always played exactly right, but I always did play loud and real heavy.
You think most of the New Orleans fellas played pretty heavy, would you say?

Well, no, we have quite a few of them that play soft bass. I mean, you take, for instance, McClane. I think he's got a soft touch. He's a nice bass player, a real nice bass, but he's, he plays a soft bass. I think he's got an amplifier now. An amplifier would help him. I don't think he uses it in the paddock. No. But he's a, he's a fine bass man, but he's a very soft man. Rick Hart plays soft too most of the time. He, he carries an amplifier. Yeah. But I just don't like the, the amplified bass. I don't care too much for the fender. But, uh, if Dixon Land music don't pick up for me, as soon as I can go to rock and roll, I have to get a fender, because that's all they want now.

What about the laminated wood? You mentioned that once. Do you think that, can you tell the difference between the old style construction, carved out of one big thick piece of wood, they start the big thing four or five inches thick when they make them right?

Oh, there's a different tonation there. That's the, real tone itself, that wood. I mean, of course, the thing I got, I mean, is the plywood bass. I mean, just my heavy playing, I guess, that brings up the tone the way it did. But I mean, uh, it sounds good to me. Well, it's natural wood bass. I mean, uh, nice. The same as a guitar. I mean, you got a guitar, one of them old guitars that's a natural wood. You got a beautiful instrument, a beautiful sounding instrument. But you get those, uh, these modern guitars, they all plywood with, uh, all this mechanism. Oh, wash bone. Yeah. I mean, anything. They make them out of compressed paper, I guess, most of the time. Wash bone. Good dread wood. Wash bone. Well, that's just a block in here from compressed paper.
Say, I was wondering, uh, the other questions, they're going to have about a half a minute left.
Did you admire any drummers that caused you to start on drums, particular?

No, I don't know how I got tangled up with the drum. At that time, I don't think I was any more than about 11 or 12 years old. And, uh, I just wanted to get in the band. I didn't care what I played. You know, I imagine that's the way I must have felt. You didn't hang around the big 25 or
anything at that time. And you were a little young to go out and hear those times.

No, I do remember, uh, Joe Snye and myself, we lied about our age to go to the entertainers and watch Bucket play drum. He was a wonderful drummer. Pity to him. Yeah, he had a lot of novelty with him, you know, stick tricks and all that kind of stuff. And then, uh, we had to go to the entertainers and watch Bucket play drum. He was a wonderful drummer. Pity to him. Pity to him. Yeah, he had a lot of novelty with him, you know, stick tricks and all that kind of stuff. And, uh, well, I used to like the way old Ransom played at the bass. I always liked his playing fine bass man.
Well, I can't think of any other questions. Anything you'd like to add? Anything about your life? You think we might have forgotten? Otherwise, we're just about at the end.
Oh, no, it's just about all of them. I'm playing with Lawrence Morell, the Dixieland band. All we need is some customers. We've got the band.
Yeah, that's right. It's a good band. We're trying to line that up, we hope.
It's still playing. I mean, uh, uh, I'd like to get my hand on the bass too, but I can push some bass too, but through a Dixieland band a little bit. I imagine it's just sound pretty good. I'm fast.
Yeah, I like the bass violin. You do? The bass violin. The bass violin has a real volume.
I had a tuba here two weeks ago or three weeks ago, maybe. Was that an E flat? Yeah, it was a big E flat. Nice big. Good stuff.
